card.summary_ko: 1766년(음력) 2월 23일, 홍대용이 김재행과 함께 베이징 건정동 숙소에서 엄성·반정균을 다시 만나고 육비를 처음 만난 하루의 필담. 이별의 충고, 주자학과 육학 논쟁, 금주령 아래의 술자리 이야기가 이어진다.
card.summary_en: Brush talk from the 23rd day of the second lunar month of 1766, when Hong Dae-yong and Kim Jae-haeng revisit Yan Cheng and Pan Tingyun at their Beijing lodging and meet Lu Fei for the first time: parting advice, a Zhu Xi versus Lu school debate, and a drinking party despite Joseon's wine ban.

notes.ko:
**저자** 홍대용(洪大容, 1731-1783, 호 담헌)은 노론 계열 양반 집안 출신으로, 노론 학자 김원행에게 배웠다. 과거에는 합격하지 못하고 천거로 관직에 나아가 훗날 지방 수령을 지냈다. 박지원·박제가와 함께 북학(北學)파로 꼽히며, 조정이 여전히 청나라를 오랑캐로 얕보던 때에 청의 기술과 제도를 배워야 한다고 주장했다. 나경적과 함께 혼천의를 만들었고, 후기 저술 『의산문답』 등에서 지구가 자전한다고 주장하며 중국만이 세계의 중심이라는 생각을 의문시했고, 화이(華夷)의 구별을 상대화하는 견해로 이어졌다. 이 글에서는 여전히 주자를 옹호하며, 그가 성리학 정통에서 얼마나 벗어났는지는 연구자마다 평가가 갈린다.

**시대적 맥락** 1765-66년 겨울 홍대용은 서장관이던 숙부 홍억을 따라 자제군관 자격으로 연행사 일행과 함께 베이징에 갔다. 조선은 공식적으로 만주족의 청을 멸시했지만 해마다 사신을 보냈고, 그는 이례적으로 한족 선비를 적극 찾아 나섰다. 벗 김재행(평중)과 함께 회시를 보러 와 있던 저장(浙江) 출신 엄성(역암)·반정균(난공)을 만났고, 이어 육비(기잠, 호 소음)를 만났다. 이후 편지로 이어진 이 우정은 국경을 넘은 교유의 대표 사례가 되었고, 박지원 등 북학파 문인에게 영향을 주었다고 전한다.

**배경** 담헌 홍대용의 문집 『담헌서』 외집에 실린 「건정동필담」(乾淨衕筆談, 중국 선비들의 숙소가 있던 골목)에 속한 글이다. 대화는 대체로 종이에 써서 나누었고 일부는 말로도 오갔다. 이 리더 텍스트는 표제와 앞의 13개 문단, 곧 1766년(병술) 2월 23일 하루의 기록만 싣는다. 육비를 처음 만나는 날이며, 24일부터 29일까지는 싣지 않았다. 원문은 중문 위키문헌 「湛軒書/外集卷三」(판본 2427369)의 전사본이다. 머리말 서식에 연도 1939가 적혀 있어 1939년 활자본 『담헌서』(신조선사 간으로 알려짐)를 바탕으로 한 것으로 보이나, 위키문헌이 판본을 자세히 밝히지는 않는다. 날짜는 모두 음력이다.

**의의** 조선과 청 문인의 교유를 가장 생생하게 보여 주는 장면으로, 솔직하고 익살스럽고 눈물겹고 술에 취한 모습이 모두 들어 있다. 주자학과 육구연의 학문을 둘러싼 토론, 주자가 『시경』 소서(小序)를 버린 일에 대한 논쟁도 남아 있다.

**형식과 주제** 편지와 시가 끼어 있는 대화 기록으로, 평이한 한문에 구어 표현이 조금 섞여 있다. 주제는 첫 만남에서 맺는 지기(知己)의 정, 나이에 따른 형제 결의, 벗 사이의 직언, 조선의 금주령과 중국의 음주, 두 유학 학파의 차이다.

**읽기 도움**
- 筆談(필담): 글로 써서 나누는 대화.
- 解元(해원): 향시 수석 합격자. 여기서는 육비.
- 炕(항): 구들처럼 덥힌 벽돌 침상으로 의자처럼 쓴다.
- 訂交(정교): 벗으로 사귐을 정함. 贈言(증언): 이별할 때 주는 충고의 말.
- 小序(소서): 『시경』의 소서. 주자는 이를 버렸다.
- 尊德性 / 道問學: 육구연과 주자 각각이 중시한 면.
- 邦禁(방금): 나라의 금령, 여기서는 금주령.
- 馬脚(마각): 말의 다리, 곧 정체가 드러남.
- 時中之聖: '때에 맞게 처신하는 성인', 홍대용을 놀리는 말.
- 반정균의 호 '추고'(秋庫)는 원문에서 이체자 秋𢈢로 적혀 있다.

번역은 AI가 했고 불확실한 곳은 괄호로 표시했다. 『시경』 학파를 가리키는 '高魯韓'은 원문 전사 과정의 오류로 보이며 '齊魯韓'일 가능성이 크다. '次公'은 『한서』의 개관요(蓋寬饒, 자 차공)를 가리키는 말로 '술 없이도 미쳤다'는 농담이다. '桂磄酒'(술 이름)와 '奪陸兄今日之政'은 뜻이 확실하지 않아 번역에 그렇게 밝혔다.
notes.en:
**About the author** Hong Dae-yong (1731-1783, style Damheon) came from a yangban family of the Noron faction and studied under the Noron scholar Kim Won-haeng. He did not pass the civil-service examinations; he entered office through recommendation and later served as a county magistrate. He is counted among the "Northern Learning" (Bukhak) thinkers, with Park Ji-won and Park Je-ga, who argued that Joseon should learn techniques and institutions from Qing China even though officialdom still looked down on the Manchu dynasty. With Na Gyeong-jeok he built an armillary sphere and, in later writings such as the Uisan mundap, argued that the earth rotates and questioned the view that China alone is the centre of the world, a line of thought that relativised the Chinese/barbarian distinction. In this text he still defends Zhu Xi, and scholars disagree about how far he broke with Neo-Confucian orthodoxy.

**Historical context** In the winter of 1765-66 Hong went to Beijing with the Joseon embassy as an unofficial attendant (jaje gunggwan) of his uncle Hong Eok, the embassy's secretary (seojanggwan). Joseon officially despised the Manchu Qing, but it sent embassies every year. Hong, unusually, sought out Han Chinese scholars. With his friend Kim Jae-haeng (Pyeongjung) he met Yan Cheng (Li'an) and Pan Tingyun (Langong), Zhejiang scholars in the capital for the examinations, and later Lu Fei (Qiqian, "Xiaoyin"). Their friendship, kept up by letters, became a famous example of friendship across borders and is said to have influenced Park Ji-won and others.

**Background** The piece comes from Hong's "Brush Conversations at Ganjing Alley" (the Chinese scholars' lodging), in the outer collection (oejip) of the Damheon seo, the collected works of Hong Dae-yong. The speakers wrote on paper, and some exchanges were also spoken. This Reader text keeps the heading and the first 13 paragraphs: one single day, the 23rd of the second month of 1766 (the bingxu year), when Lu Fei is first met. The remaining days (24th-29th) are not shown. The text is Chinese Wikisource's transcription of "湛軒書/外集卷三" (revision 2427369); its Header template gives only the year 1939, which suggests the 1939 printed edition of the Damheon seo (reportedly from Sin Joseon-sa), but Wikisource does not describe the edition in detail. All dates are lunar.

**Significance** The scene is one of the liveliest records of Joseon-Qing literati contact: frank, joking, tearful and drunken. It also preserves a debate between Zhu Xi's and Lu Jiuyuan's schools and a dispute over Zhu Xi's rejection of the Minor Prefaces of the Odes.

**Form and themes** A dialogue transcript with letters and poems embedded, in plain classical Chinese with a few colloquial touches. Themes: instant friendship ("knowing one another"), oaths of brotherhood by age, honest criticism between friends, Joseon's wine ban versus Chinese drinking, and the two Confucian schools.

**Reading help**
- 筆談 (pildam): conversation conducted by writing.
- 解元 (haewon): a provincial-examination top graduate; here Lu Fei.
- 炕 (hang): heated brick platform bed, used as a seat.
- 訂交 (jeonggyo): to pledge friendship; 贈言 (jeungeon): parting words of advice.
- 小序 (soseo): the "Minor Prefaces" of the Book of Odes; Zhu Xi discarded them.
- 尊德性 / 道問學: "honouring the moral nature" / "the path of inquiry and study", the Lu and Zhu emphases.
- 邦禁 (bang-geum): national ban, here on alcohol.
- 馬脚 (magak): "horse's hoof", i.e. giving oneself away.
- 時中之聖: "sage of timeliness", a teasing title for Hong.
- Pan Tingyun's sobriquet "Qiuku" (秋庫) is written in the source with a variant character (秋𢈢).

The translation is by AI; uncertain passages are flagged in brackets or parentheses. "高魯韓" (for the Odes schools) is probably a copying error for "Qi, Lu, Han" in the source. "次公" alludes to Gai Kuanrao of the Han (courtesy name Cigong) and the joke that he was wild even when sober; the liquor name "桂磄酒" and the phrase "奪陸兄今日之政" remain uncertain and are flagged as such in the translation.

paragraphs.en: ## Brush Conversations at Ganjing Alley, Continued

paragraphs.orig: 二十三日。門禁解。與平仲往。有客在座。逡巡不欲遽進。蘭公出門歡迎曰不妨。遂同入則力闇又爲相携就坐。見炕上有綃畫幾幅書帙堆散。蘭公有忙色曰。昨日。陸解元到京。弟以吾輩訂交唱和事。一一詳言之。並出詩札相示。渠聞之。悵恨到京之遲。不得訂交。卽于燈下作畫五幅及札一通。擬呈三大人及二兄。其人高雅絶世。同在此間。可以相會。如何。余曰。此作蓮花詩者陸先生耶。蘭公喜曰然。余曰。見其詩願見而不可得。天幸近臨。豈非吾輩之厚緣。力闇曰。此公吾輩所仰重者。其人品學術。足爲吾輩師法。乃以其書示之。書曰。陸飛啓。此行自恨來遲。不及一親言論風采。生平第一缺陷事也。午後甫克解鞍客邸。入門未及他語。力闇秋𢈢卽歷叙與諸公往來情事。亹亹不休。幷出諸公手跡長篇短頁。縱橫几案。觸目琳琅。應接不暇。力闇秋𢈢又從傍稱述種種。耳目俱勞。兩官並用。又如讀龍門佳傳。夾叙事狀。議論傾倒。忭舞莫可言狀。聞諸公使事有緖。將次就道。形格勢阻。想怱怱不獲一出。而飛又初到此間。俗務糾纏。漫無條理。恐終無見理也。但生平以朋友爲命。况値海上異人。且不止一人。如竟不獲附力闇秋𢈢之末。則此二人者。飛終身抱不解之妬矣。膓熱如火。一版傾寫之意。無可發泄。遂忘其拙。用絹五幅。燃燭作畫。聊代羔雁。畫竟。時漏下已三皷。工拙不足言。但此時濡筆揮灑。不特忘日間車馬之勞。幷不覺更漏之促。其心可想矣。人生會合。定是有緣有數。不可勉强。然安知今日不會。非他日相見之根。安知此生不會。再世不大會乎。見後相思與不見相思。同一無窮。而不見之相思。更深於見。且有相思之致而無離別之苦。省却多少兒女之態。正不必定以相見不相見較優劣也。譬之讀古人書。古人豈可見而尙友之志則如或見之。使此生白首數千里外。各各胸中有某名某姓其人。則飛與諸公。皆未往之古人也。何幸如之。拙稿五册並呈分諸公。此飛臨行時猝刻也。不特字蹟潦草。且多錯誤。未及校正。其一切未妥處。祈進而敎之。稿中有題自畫荷風竹露草堂圖。是飛敝廬。不拘詩文。能各賜一篇。拜貺良多。有忠天廟畫壁歌。能各賜一篇。則跪拜受之。感且不朽。陸飛再拜啓。丙戌二月二十二日夜。看畢。平仲大喜曰。弟等當趍拜。蘭公曰。何必進去。卽走出。余與平仲出未及門。陸解元已掀簾而入矣。爲人軀榦短少而肥面白晢。風儀偉然。向吾輩微笑。擧手而揖。余肅揖致敬。解元以手扶策之。至炕下讓登。力闇曰。都係至好。遠客上坐。平仲曰。同爲客也。何擇遠近。只以年齒爲先。余謂平仲。且徇俗。不必以虛禮相拘。余遂與平仲先登。負壁坐于卓之左右。解元坐于余之下。蘭公坐于平仲之下。力闇別以椅子。當炕而坐。余曰。仰聲久矣。幸此承顔。驚喜之極。第蒙謬愛。愧無以仰答。平仲曰。海隅鯫生。偶入中國。獲拜二友。遂爲知己。頃覽瓊篇。願一見之。不意今日瞻望雅儀。此必有神鬼之助也。解元曰。昨日一到。卽傾倒欲狂。自分不得相見。得見實屬非常之幸。余曰。吾輩歸期。决以初一。不料其遷就若是。歸心如箭。宜其爲欝。惟以更會二兄。尙有餘期爲幸。今又獲拜陸先生。是天與之便。解元曰。昨。力闇秋𢈢。極道理學大儒。願爲弟子不暇。今忽此稱呼。是鄙棄我耶。余曰。今承盛敎。非我棄長者。長者棄我也。諸人皆笑。解元曰。如此。便糾纏世故不了矣。竟訂交何如。余曰。敢不惟命。解元曰。我年四十八。金公貴庚多少。平仲曰。四十九。解元曰。吾兄也。平仲曰。不敢辭也。解元又問余曰。貴庚多少。余曰。三十六。解元曰。然則吾弟也。余笑曰。亦不敢辭也。諸人皆笑。余曰。此會。實千古奇緣。陸解元字起潛。號篠飮。起潛曰。力闇與我等。雖入名塲。本無榮慕。今日便是此生絶大遭逢。誠如所言。余曰。陸丈開懷喜接。可見長者風。起潛曰。人世難逢開口笑。見諸公不得不喜。余曰。金兄麁心大談。絶無東國氣味。此可爲兄輩所取。起潛笑而指麁心大談四字曰。是我輩。力闇以詩稿五册。綃畫五幅示我輩曰。陸兄詩稿。送三大人三本。二兄分領一本。其五幅綃畫。亦如之。蘭公展其畫而示之。皆水墨亂草。筆畫雄偉。蘭公指二幅畫曰。此瀑布此雲氣。盖益奇壯也。力闇曰。此皆昨夜燈下所畫。至三更始畢。余看畢曰。謹當領歸。若奉圭璧。只恨踈拙無以贊揚。此是遊藝之一端。宜不足爲盛德之能事。知者觀其心畫。亦或窺其萬一。昔宋時。域外問朱先生安否。傳者至今榮之。如是則外國有尊仰之者。益有光於君子。歸以傳之海東。佇見他日有問陸先生安否也。起潛曰。小道僅供遊戲。何足爲輕重。雕蟲篆刻。丈夫不爲。徒取笑耳。如海東。亦須此覆醬瓿則可矣。余與平仲看其詩稿。起潛曰。拙稿。此時不必看且談。平仲曰。弟於凡事。庸陋極矣。今於瓊篇不敢辭聞一知十也。起潛曰。昨讀大作。豪逸眞切。蘇長公之流也。拜服拜服。平仲曰。不敢。何其過褒之若是也。起潛指其詩稿中忠天廟詩曰。忠天廟。是里社中祀。社神是隋唐時越國公汪華。後殿畫壁。是先曾祖手蹟。乞諸公不拘詩文寵光。當勒石不朽。力闇曰。洪兄不喜作詩。竟懇其作騷體數韻何如。洪兄騷體。不减屈宋也。起潛曰。屈子忠愛。亦是道學。余曰。謹與金兄歸而圖之於行前。但平生於著述。拙澁無雙。恐不及搆出耳。余曰。願聞壁畫是何物。先先生平日行跡略示之。兼以寓尊仰之意。起潛曰。壁畫是諸天神佛。今已糢糊不復可辨。先曾祖諱瀚字少微號雪酣道人。値明季隱於畫。壽亦不長。別無見于時。畫名至今在人口。但贋本甚多。拙詩中已具大略。尊仰之意不敢當。但以我輩相遇之情作原起及見拙詩有此題云云可矣。西湖爲吾杭名勝。諸兄定必神𨓏。或以此作波瀾何如。平仲曰。弟在東國。聞西湖名勝。神往者已久。而每歎無路一見破此宿願。何幸今日。遇闇蘭二兄。披襟瀉懷。已至忘形。所謂西湖十景。風斯在下。志氣暢快。其樂無窮。雖不見錢塘。亦無所恨。又得陸兄於二兄之座。天下豈有如此樂事。但筆不如舌。猶不能傾瀉所蘊。是可恨也。所示事。當極意仰副。而今來大國。若非兄輩。或能全其拙而歸矣。以兄之故。弟之醜陋。秋毫不能掩。作天下愚弄之人。此所謂靡君之故。胡爲乎泥中者也。諸人皆笑。力闇曰。其家有荷風竹露草堂。前植叢篠。後一大池。遍種芙蓉。羣書揷架。籤秩縱橫。此公偃仰其中。享盡人間淸福。不可不乞一語以題其草堂。起潛曰。三大人亦望爲我乞言可乎。余曰。當致盛意。起潛謂余曰。聞兄宗朱。我則陸學。奈何。余曰。陸先生之學。非陸學而何。諸人大笑。余曰。陸丈是象山之後耶。曰不然。力闇曰。前日書贈尊德性二語。終身佩服。起潛曰。此是正論。原不當分爲二。余曰。鄙書是已陳蒭狗。何足爲奇。不當分二之敎。恐是不易之論。余又曰。弟於二兄。妄有贈別語數十字。方在懷中。兼以請敎於陸丈可乎。起潛曰。丈丈不休。何也。始終見棄耶。余曰。年丈十二。非丈耶。是乃兄事之也。起潛曰。我國不然。丈尊於兄。後竟稱兄。余曰。東俗。平交始稱兄。恐各從其俗力闇請見贈語。余出諸懷中而與之。起潛展讀之。其贈蘭公曰。

paragraphs.en:
The twenty-third day. The gate restrictions were lifted. I went with Pyeongjung. There were guests seated inside, and I hesitated, not wishing to enter abruptly. Langong came out of the door to welcome us, saying, "It is no matter." So we went in together, and Li'an again took us by the hand and seated us. On the kang I saw several silk paintings and books and booklets heaped and scattered about. Langong, with a flustered look, said, "Yesterday Lu the Jieyuan arrived in the capital. I told him everything, one by one, of how we have formed our friendship and exchanged poems, and I showed him the poems and letters as well. When he heard it, he lamented that he had come to the capital so late and could not make friends with you. At once, under the lamp, he painted five pictures and wrote a letter, intending to present them to the three Excellencies and to you two brothers. He is a man of lofty refinement, matchless in his age. He is staying here in the same place, so you could meet him. What do you say?"

I said, "Is this the Master Lu who wrote the lotus poem?" Langong said happily, "Yes." I said, "Having read his poems I longed to see him but could not; that heaven's good fortune brings him close to us now, is it not a generous fate for us?" Li'an said, "This gentleman is one whom we revere. His character, learning and scholarship are enough to be a model for us." He then showed us Lu's letter. The letter said:

"Lu Fei respectfully reports. On this journey I regret that I came so late and did not get to be close to your conversation and bearing; it is the foremost deficiency of my life. In the afternoon I had only just unsaddled at my lodging, and before I could say anything else on entering the door, Li'an and Qiuku at once recounted in order their dealings with you gentlemen, tirelessly, and brought out your handwriting, long pieces and short leaves, strewn across the table, a feast of gems wherever the eye fell, more than I could take in. Li'an and Qiuku, standing by, praised you in many ways, tiring ear and eye alike, two organs working at once; it was like reading a fine biography by Longmen [Sima Qian], narrating events interleaved with discussion pouring forth. I danced for joy beyond description.

"I hear that your envoys' business is reaching a conclusion and you will soon set out on the road. With circumstances hindering and obstructing, I suppose you are in a rush and will not manage to come out; and I too have only just arrived here, entangled in worldly business and in complete disorder, so I fear that in the end there is no prospect of meeting. But all my life I have taken friends as my very life, and now especially I have met extraordinary men from beyond the sea, and more than one. If in the end I cannot attach myself to the tail of Li'an and Qiuku, then toward those two men I shall bear an undying envy for the rest of my life. My heart burns like fire; the feelings I would pour out on a single sheet have no outlet. So, forgetting my clumsiness, I took five lengths of silk, lit a candle and painted, to serve in place of the lamb and the goose [the gifts of introduction]. When the painting was done, the water-clock had already struck the third drum. Whether it is skilled or clumsy is not worth mentioning, but at this moment, as I dipped my brush and swept it about, I forgot not only the fatigue of the day's carriages and horses but even the hurrying of the night hours; you can imagine my feelings.

"In human life, meetings are surely a matter of fate and destiny and cannot be forced. Yet who knows whether not meeting today may not be the root of meeting another day? Who knows whether not meeting in this life may not be a great meeting in the next? Longing after meeting and longing without meeting are equally endless, and the longing of not meeting is deeper than that of meeting. Moreover, there is the savour of longing without the pain of parting, sparing much of the behaviour of sentimental lovers. One really need not judge better or worse by meeting or not meeting. Compare reading the books of the ancients: how can one see the ancients in person? Yet the aspiration to befriend them in spirit is as though one had seen them. If in this life we grow white-haired thousands of li apart, each with a certain name and surname held in his heart, then I and you gentlemen are each ancients not yet visited. What fortune could equal that?

"Five volumes of my poor drafts are presented together, to be divided among you gentlemen. These were hastily cut [for printing] by me as I was leaving. Not only is the calligraphy scrawled, there are also many errors, and I had no time to correct them. For all that is improper in them, I beg you to come forward and instruct me. Among the drafts is a 'Painting of the Hall of Lotus Wind and Bamboo Dew', inscribed on my own painting; that hall is my humble dwelling. Whether in poetry or prose, if each of you could grant me one piece, the favour would be great. There is also a 'Song of the Painted Wall of the Zhongtian Temple'; if each of you could grant one piece, I shall receive it kneeling, with gratitude that will never fade. Lu Fei bows twice and reports. Night of the twenty-second day of the second month of the bingxu year."

When we had finished reading, Pyeongjung was overjoyed and said, "We should go and pay our respects." Langong said, "Why need you go in?" and ran straight out. Before Pyeongjung and I had reached the door, Jieyuan Lu had already lifted the curtain and come in. He was short of stature and plump, with a fair white face and an imposing bearing. He smiled toward us, raised his hands and bowed; I bowed gravely in respect. The Jieyuan steadied me with his hand, and at the foot of the kang we yielded places to one another to climb up. Li'an said, "All here are the best of friends; the guests from afar should take the seats of honour." Pyeongjung said, "We are all guests; why choose near or far? Let age alone come first." I said to Pyeongjung, "Let us follow the custom for the moment; there is no need to be bound by empty ceremony." So Pyeongjung and I climbed up first and sat with our backs to the wall, one on each side of the table. The Jieyuan sat below me, and Langong below Pyeongjung; Li'an took a chair apart and sat facing the kang.

I said, "I have long admired your fame; to receive your countenance now is a joy that startles me to the utmost. Yet, favoured with your mistaken regard, I am ashamed to have nothing with which to answer." Pyeongjung said, "A petty fellow from a corner of the sea, I chanced to enter China and had the honour of meeting two friends, who became my bosom friends. Not long ago I read your jade-like verses and longed to see you once. I never expected to gaze today upon your elegant presence; surely gods and spirits have helped." The Jieyuan said, "As soon as I arrived yesterday I was overwhelmed with wild admiration. I had thought I could not meet you; to meet you is truly an extraordinary good fortune."

I said, "Our date of return was fixed for the first. I did not expect it to be put off like this. With a heart eager to go home like an arrow, it is natural that I was depressed. My only consolation is that I can meet you two brothers again, since some days are still left. Now I have also the honour of meeting Master Lu; this is a convenience heaven has granted."

The Jieyuan said, "Yesterday Li'an and Qiuku spoke at length of you as a great Confucian of the school of principle, and said they wished to become your disciples without delay. Now you suddenly address me with this title of respect; are you scorning me?" I said, "Having now received your instruction, it is not I who scorn the elder; it is the elder who scorns me." Everyone laughed. The Jieyuan said, "If so, we shall be tangled in worldly forms without end. Why not simply make friends?" I said, "How dare I not obey?" The Jieyuan said, "I am forty-eight. How old is Master Kim?" Pyeongjung said, "Forty-nine." The Jieyuan said, "Then you are my elder brother." Pyeongjung said, "I dare not decline." The Jieyuan then asked me, "How old are you?" I said, "Thirty-six." The Jieyuan said, "Then you are my younger brother." I said with a smile, "I dare not decline that either." Everyone laughed.

I said, "This meeting is truly a rare fate of a thousand ages." (Jieyuan Lu's courtesy name is Qiqian, and his style is Xiaoyin.) Qiqian said, "Li'an and I and the others, though we have entered the examination halls, have never craved glory. Today is the greatest encounter of this life, truly as you say." I said, "Elder Lu receives us with an open heart and joy; one can see the manner of an elder." Qiqian said, "In the human world it is hard to meet an open-mouthed laugh; seeing you gentlemen I cannot but be glad." I said, "Brother Kim speaks big with a coarse heart, utterly without the flavour of the Eastern Country [Korea]; this may be what you gentlemen value in him." Qiqian smiled and pointed at the four characters "coarse heart, big talk", saying, "That is the likes of us."

Li'an showed us the five volumes of poem drafts and the five silk paintings, saying, "Brother Lu's drafts: three copies go to the three Excellencies, and you two brothers take one copy between you. The five silk paintings likewise." Langong unrolled the paintings and showed them: all were ink-wash, in a loose cursive manner, the brushwork bold and grand. Langong pointed to two of the pictures and said, "This is a waterfall; this is cloud vapour; they are even more strange and magnificent." Li'an said, "All of these he painted last night under the lamp; he finished only at the third watch."

When I had looked them over, I said, "I shall respectfully accept them and take them home, as if bearing jade tablets. I only regret that I am too clumsy to praise them. This is one aspect of 'roaming in the arts', and it should hardly count as the proper business of a man of great virtue. One who understands will look at the painting of his heart and perhaps glimpse a ten-thousandth part of it. In Song times, people beyond the borders asked after the welfare of Master Zhu, and those who passed on the news have been honoured for it to this day. If so, then that foreigners revere you will add even more lustre to a gentleman. I shall carry this back and spread it in Haedong [Korea], and I expect to see the day when people ask after the welfare of Master Lu." Qiqian said, "A minor art, merely for amusement; what weight does it carry? Insect-carving and seal-carving are not things a man does; it only invites laughter. In Haedong too, it will do only if they use it to cover soy jars."

Pyeongjung and I looked at his poem drafts. Qiqian said, "My poor drafts need not be looked at now; let us talk." Pyeongjung said, "In everything I am extremely common and crude, but before your jewelled pieces I do not presume to decline 'hearing one and knowing ten'." Qiqian said, "Yesterday I read your honoured work: bold, unrestrained, true and heartfelt, of the school of Su Changgong [Su Shi]. I bow in admiration." Pyeongjung said, "I dare not. Why such excessive praise?" Qiqian pointed in his drafts to the poem on the Zhongtian Temple and said, "The Zhongtian Temple is the village shrine for sacrifices. The tutelary god is Wang Hua, Duke of Yue in the Sui and Tang period. The painted wall of the rear hall is the handiwork of my late great-grandfather. I beg you gentlemen, without restriction to poetry or prose, to grace it; it will be carved in stone so that it will never perish."

Li'an said, "Brother Hong does not like to write poetry. Why not earnestly ask him for a few rhymes in the Sao style? Brother Hong's Sao style is no less than that of Qu and Song." Qiqian said, "Master Qu's loyalty and love are also moral learning." I said, "I shall respectfully go back with Brother Kim and think about it before our departure. But in writing I have been unmatched in clumsiness and crudeness all my life, and I fear I shall not manage to compose it in time." I also said, "I would like to hear what the wall painting is, and to be given a brief account of your late ancestor's ordinary conduct, so as to lodge my respect in it."

Qiqian said, "The wall painting is of the heavenly deities and Buddhas; it is now blurred and can no longer be made out. My late great-grandfather, whose personal name was Han, courtesy name Shaowei, style Xuehan Daoren, lived at the end of the Ming and hid himself in painting; his life was not long, and otherwise he did not appear in his age. His fame as a painter is still on people's lips, but there are many forgeries. My poem already gives the outline. As for 'respect', I dare not accept it. It will do to take the feelings of our meeting as the opening, and to say that on seeing my poem you found this topic, and so on. West Lake is the famous scenery of my Hangzhou, and you gentlemen surely long for it in spirit. Perhaps you could use it to stir up some waves in the piece?"

Pyeongjung said, "In the Eastern Country I heard of the fame of West Lake and have long gone there in spirit, but I always lamented that there was no way to see it once and fulfil this old wish. How fortunate today to meet Brothers Yan and Pan, to open our robes and pour out our hearts until we forget ourselves. As for the Ten Views of West Lake, 'the wind is below us'; my spirit is refreshed and the joy is endless; even if I never see Qiantang I shall have no regret. And now I have also gained Brother Lu at the seat of the two brothers. How could there be such joy under heaven? Only the brush is not as good as the tongue and still cannot pour out what I hold; that is regrettable. As for the matter you have set, I shall comply with all my heart. But coming now to the Great Country, had it not been for you gentlemen, I might have gone home with my clumsiness intact. Because of you, my ugliness and coarseness cannot be hidden by the width of a hair, and I have become a man made a fool of before all the world. This is what is meant by 'were it not for you, why should I be in the mud?'" Everyone laughed.

Li'an said, "His house has the Thatched Hall of Lotus Wind and Bamboo Dew. In front are planted clumps of dwarf bamboo; behind is a large pond planted all over with lotus; books fill the shelves and labelled bundles lie crisscross. This gentleman lies and looks up amid them, enjoying to the full the pure blessings of the human world. We must beg a word to inscribe on his thatched hall." Qiqian said, "I hope the three Excellencies too will beg words for me; may I ask?" I said, "I shall convey your kind wish." Qiqian said to me, "I hear that you follow Zhu; I follow Lu's learning. What of that?" I said, "Master Lu's learning: what is it, if not Lu's learning?" Everyone laughed heartily. I said, "Is Elder Lu a descendant of Xiangshan [Lu Jiuyuan]?" He said, "No." Li'an said, "The two phrases on honouring the moral nature that you wrote for me the other day I shall carry with me all my life." Qiqian said, "That is a correct doctrine; originally it should not be divided in two." I said, "My writing is a straw dog already used; what is remarkable about it? But the instruction that it should not be divided in two is perhaps an unalterable doctrine."

I said further, "To you two brothers I have presumptuously written parting words of several dozen characters; they are in my bosom. May I also ask Elder Lu for his instruction on them?" Qiqian said, "You keep saying 'elder, elder' without stopping; why? Are you rejecting me from start to finish?" I said, "You are twelve years my senior; are you not an elder? That is treating you as an elder brother." Qiqian said, "In my country it is not so: 'elder' is more honoured than 'brother', and later one finally says 'brother'." I said, "In the Eastern custom, only equals address each other as 'brother'. I think each of us should follow his own custom." Li'an asked to see the parting words. I took them out of my bosom and gave them to him. Qiqian unrolled and read them. What I had presented to Langong said:

paragraphs.orig: 仁者之別。必贈以言。余何敢當。雖然。吾輩將生死別矣。其無可言乎。
paragraphs.reading: 인자지별. 필증이언. 여하감당. 수연. 오배장생사별의. 기무가언호.
paragraphs.en: When a benevolent man parts from one, he must give words as a parting gift. How dare I presume to be one? Yet we are about to part as if for life and death. Could there be nothing to say?

paragraphs.orig: 太上修己而安人。其次善道而立敎。最下者著書而圖不朽。外此者求利達而已。苟求利達而已。亦將何所不至哉。
paragraphs.reading: 태상수기이안인. 기차선도이립교. 최하자저서이도불후. 외차자구이달이이. 구구이달이이. 역장하소부지재.
paragraphs.en: The highest is to cultivate oneself and so bring peace to others; next is to master the Way and establish teaching; the lowest is to write books and seek immortality. Beyond these are only those who seek profit and advancement. And if one merely seeks profit and advancement, to what will one not come?

paragraphs.orig: 仕有時乎爲榮。亦有時乎爲恥。立乎人之本朝而志不在乎三代之禮樂。是爲容悅也。是爲富且貴也。此而不知恥。其難與言矣。
paragraphs.reading: 사유시호위영. 역유시호위치. 입호인지본조이지부재호삼대지예악. 시위용열야. 시위부차귀야. 차이부지치. 기난여언의.
paragraphs.en: Office is sometimes an honour and sometimes a disgrace. To stand in another man's court with one's aim not set on the rites and music of the Three Dynasties is mere ingratiation, mere being rich and honoured. If one does not know shame in this, it is hard to speak with him.

paragraphs.orig: 有高才能文章而無德以將之。或贏得薄倖名。或陷爲輕薄子。若是乎才不可恃而德不可緩也。
paragraphs.en: One who has high talent and can write, but has no virtue to lead it, either wins a name for heartlessness or falls into being a frivolous fellow. Thus talent cannot be relied upon and virtue must not be put off.

paragraphs.orig: 非寡欲無以養心。非威重無以善學。任重而道遠。凡我同志。奈何不敬。
paragraphs.en: Without few desires there is no nourishing the heart; without dignity and gravity there is no learning well. The burden is heavy and the road is long. All of us who share one aim, how can we not be reverent?

paragraphs.orig: 善惡萌於中而吉凶著於外。如欲進德而修業。盖亦反求諸己而已矣。
paragraphs.en: Good and evil sprout within, and good and ill fortune show themselves without. If one wishes to advance in virtue and cultivate one's work, it is simply a matter of turning back and seeking it in oneself.

paragraphs.orig: 起潛看畢曰。寫一張與我。作座右銘常目。又曰。竟是正蒙。不特其文之似而已。又讀贈力闇語曰。

paragraphs.orig: 維杭有山。可採可茹。維杭有水。可濯可漁。文武之道。布在方册。可卷而舒。子弟從之。可觀厥成。優哉遊哉。可以終吾生。

paragraphs.en: In Hang there are mountains; one may gather and eat from them. In Hang there are waters; one may wash in them and fish in them. The Way of Wen and Wu is spread out in the books on bamboo slips; it may be rolled up and unrolled. If the sons and younger brothers follow it, one may see its achievement. Be at ease, roam at leisure; thus one may end one's life.

paragraphs.orig: 夫道一則專。專則靜。靜則明生焉。明生焉而物乃照矣。
paragraphs.en: When the Way is one, it is focused; when focused, it is still; when still, brightness is born; and when brightness is born, things are illumined.

paragraphs.orig: 止水明鑑。體之立也。開物成務。用之達也。專於體者。佛氏之逃空也。專於用者。俗儒之趍利也。

paragraphs.en: Still water as a bright mirror is the establishment of the substance; opening things and completing affairs is the reaching of the function. Those who specialise in substance are the Buddhists, who flee into emptiness; those who specialise in function are the vulgar Confucians, who run after profit.

paragraphs.orig: 朱子後孔子也。微夫子。吾誰與歸。雖然。依㨾苟同者佞也。强意立異者賊也。

paragraphs.en: Zhu Xi was the Confucius after Confucius. Were it not for that Master, with whom would I side? Yet to agree by copying the pattern is flattery, and to force a difference is to be a brigand.

paragraphs.orig: 看畢。力闇喜色溢於貌。以隷字書于簡面曰。湛軒先生臨別贈言。垂示後孫。永以爲寶。蘭公憮然少頃曰。大訓眞乃對症之藥。當終身敬佩。余曰。弟於二兄。愛之切故望之深。義在納誨。不敢爲遊辭讚歎。言雖蕪拙。其義則有稽。幸勿以人廢言。力闇曰。弟謹以作終身韋絃之佩。但見贈蘭兄語。深切著明。不特爲蘭兄對症之藥。而弟亦讀之悚然。更望作一小幅。不必佳紙。但重吾兄手蹟。俾得粘之座右。觸目警心。念玆在玆。庶幾稍有進益。則拜兄之賜更大矣。卽弟亦頗於威重二字有缺。余曰。古云有諸己而後求諸人。若是則己所不能者。終不可以責之於友乎。請諸兄明敎之。蘭公曰。箴規見古人之誼。但必繼以謙辭。則猶涉世情也。余曰。此是泛論道理。力闇曰。卽使誠如尊敎。則亦當不以人廢言。况以兄之誠中形外者耶。余曰。有諸己求諸人。恐與責善相將之義。並行而不悖。若以己不能而終不可以責諸友。則不幾於交相瘉乎。恐責乎人而己亦因此而自勉。乃不悖古義。未知如何。力闇曰。今時能以古義相勖者寥寥矣。卽無諸己而能作爾語者亦少。吾兄自以爲無諸己而責諸人。弟則以爲兄固有諸己而求諸人者也。此後不必多謙。起潛曰。摠是責善二字盡之。原不必論有無。平仲有詩曰。金玉其人錦繡膓。西湖秀氣見潘郞。公車一擢聲名早。客舘初迎坐處香。自喜奇逢應有助。只憐佳會未能長。平生作別常無淚。今日同君灑夕陽。平仲曰。此乃別潘兄之詩。幸賜批敎也。蘭公曰。詩與情。俱令人涕泗。然首四句。未免過褒。起潛笑曰。今公見女子。亦作女子態耶。盖以蘭公貌類婦人也。諸人皆大笑。力闇曰。此二紙係他人。仰慕法書。不拘幾字。隨意一揮應之。欵書尊名。平仲曰。是何敎也。弟筆醜陋。只可表情而已。言未畢。兩人又苦請不已。余亦勸之。平仲乃以半行各書唐詩一絶。皆稱好不已。平仲曰。不能違命。自處以善書。恣意揮灑。人間又有如此狂率者乎。二兄適足使愚弟露盡馬脚而少不惜焉。還爲慨然。蘭公大笑曰。正欲使兄如此。以供笑謔耳。力闇曰。弟以爲張長史不是過也。蘭公又戱曰。敎云馬脚。吾兄妙腕。乃與驥足爭能耶。平仲曰。馬脚二字之妄發甘受焉。蘭公曰。兄作書有追風逐電之勢。馬脚二字。乃絶妙評語。非妄語也。平仲謂力闇曰。頃惠養虛記。可謂擲地作金石聲。然東方邦禁至嚴。酒之一字。初不行於國中矣。旣受吾兄之文字。不但深藏篋中。以爲傳寶。亦欲誇耀人目。與知者道。此乃人情之常也。未知將奈何。力闇曰。然則另撰一篇。諱却酒字耶。酒亦何必諱。論語言酒不一。然則孔子非耶。平仲曰。嗜酒之酒。不必改。飮酒之酒。决不可少去模棱而不顯言之也。力闇曰。文章波瀾。不無假借。若去飮邊高趣。頗少興致。今早。陸兄亦獨賞此段。去之。似减風味矣。起潛曰。不言邦禁。但以近止酒爲言。何如。平仲曰。止酒二字。非老實矣。起潛曰。然則無可如何矣。力闇曰。金兄嗜酒而邦禁如此之嚴。何以過日耶。平仲曰。生不如死矣。起潛大笑曰。酒鬼。一座大笑。力闇曰。傷哉傷哉。速死投生中國爲幸。蘭公曰。若生中國。宜生于浙江。有紹興酒。日日可飮。起潛曰。我亦欲東遊如此。我以海東爲白蓮社矣。力闇曰。金兄必屢屢潛飮者。吾將出首。故以記文揚其惡耳。諸人皆笑。蘭公曰。前日弟札云。只用管仲之器。今日請用管仲如何。平仲曰。非但管仲之器。雖蠡管之用。無可奈何。又曰。拘於邦禁。自挫風味。可悲矣。起潛曰。洪兄涓滴不近口耶。余曰。素不飮。非徒守禁。起潛曰。然則並惡人飮耶。余笑曰。我自不飮。何可惡人飮酒。直惡不顧邦禁者耳。諸人皆笑。起潛曰。作離騷者。本自獨醒。蘭公曰。今日潛飮如何。平仲曰。洪兄每戒之。故洪兄在坐。不敢言酒。今日則洪兄亦無奈我何矣。起潛曰。燕會何以爲歡。余曰。十餘年間國內荐匈。禁酒甚嚴。但此終非永禁之物。故嗜之者亦多潛飮。盖以其罪不至於死也。燕會則無敢公然用之。以此時象蕭索。少樂世風味。然無可奈何矣。起潛曰。近來亦豐稔有年否。余曰。近年不甚匈歉而以禁之已久。姑不變舊耳。余曰。今日之會。無酒不可以爲歡。雖有邦禁。旣在疆域之外。亦或有從權之道。於金兄則雖不必勸之飮。亦不欲挽而沮之矣。酒鬼易魘人。如令一醉酸餘則幸矣。諸人皆笑。起潛曰。如此許之飮矣。飮後見三大人無妨否。余曰。有天下奇會。當以天下奇事應之。何可執一論也。蘭公曰。歡伯至矣。請停筆墨。遂設蔬果及肉湯數器于卓。各置小鍾于前。僕人煖酒而斟之。時有客至。余起而欲下。皆挽而止之。客卽就坐。蘭公曰。此山西韓兄。聞二兄名故來訪。力闇曰。此山西友。亦是會試同寓者。余略以語叙寒暄。其人驚謂力闇曰。他也會說我們的話。力闇有答語。槩言字同而音異。土話之不同。彼我一也。起潛曰。金兄能飮幾何而醉。余曰。他戶頗寬。但數鐘亦醉。多發狂言。平仲曰。其狂不可及。起潛曰。次公不飮而狂。何必酒。平仲曰。不飮而狂。飮後反不狂。起潛曰。海東昔日酒何酒。亦如紅毛燒酒類耶。余曰。東方多稻米。故酒亦稱美。紅露諸種。俱有其稱。桂磄酒者甚烈。嗜飮多傷人。平仲曰。大抵東國之酒峻烈。倍勝於中國。起潛曰。近來交趾桂眞者絶貴。海東所作牛皮膏及淸心丸。是眞交趾桂耶。余曰。肉桂則絶已久矣。但以皮之厚者代之。皆買於京市。其眞假何以知之。起潛曰。皮厚者。此間不重。摠以肉厚爲貴。余曰。南邊尙有眞肉桂耶。起潛曰。眞者竟難得。皮厚之桂。此間治疾。斷不敢用。是以用亦甚小。以眞者引火歸源。假者發火。東國所用。旣非眞肉桂。用之不發火耶。余曰。雖無形現之害。安知其無潛滋暗長耶。起潛曰。東國藥料。俱購自中國。亦別有土產。余曰。出自土產。可是十之爲六七。起潛曰。航海行幾日。不以爲苦耶。平仲曰。前朝則遼東路塞。故航海矣。今則只渡鴨江。大抵去京爲三千七百里矣。起潛曰。去遼東幾許。余曰。五百餘里。起潛曰。東國藏書。前朝實錄以及野史。頗備否。余曰。明史及本末等書。多有出去者。野史亦或有之。此時各以小鍾隨飮隨斟。蘭公親執一鍾。置余前而勸余曰。請飮三杯。不敢多勸。余曰。弟則素不飮矣。不必强之。且但識酒中趣。何必杯中物。起潛曰。我代飮。諸人皆笑。平仲曰。欲代洪兄。是欲倍飮也。吾與洪兄同來。欲奪陸兄今日之政耳。起潛曰。然則我幷代金兄如何。滿座皆絶倒。余呼茶。每諸人飮酒。必呼茶代之曰。以茶代酒。弟之風流。掃地盡矣。起潛曰。兄衣四面俱開。亦是前明制耶。余曰。此乃戎服。似是明制而不敢質言。官者朝服及士子道袍。大抵襲明制耳。力闇曰。前日書久未答。終當有以報之。小序决不可廢。朱子於詩注。實多蹖駁。不敢從同也。蘭公曰。朱子廢小序。多本鄭漁仲。余曰。漁仲誰也。蘭公曰。名樵號夾漈。閩人。有通志。余曰。弟則於小序。非敢蹈襲前言。非敢掩護朱子。看其言儘無據。幸兄詳示以破蒙。起潛曰。老弟宗朱極是。然廢小序。必不能强解也。蘭公曰。卽如白駒之詩。朱子注云嘉客猶逍遙也。朱子注如此類極多。果是耶。余曰。訓詁諒有餘憾。終不掩其大體之好。起潛曰。此事甚少。然此類甚多。卽以小序論。馬端臨詆朱不遺餘力。其言甚辨。以鄙意論之。小序去古不遠。似有所本。古人師授。一脉相傳。如高魯韓三家。各有所本。其實分道揚鏕。當時存之。學宮俱不廢。此不特見古人尊經。亦是信以傳信。疑以傳疑之意。而朱子斷以己意。始廢小序。其實他處宗小序頗多。獨于鄭衛則據鄭聲淫一語。遂幷置爲淫詩。聲淫非詩淫。昔人已辨之矣。如以爲淫。則夫子刪詩。本以敎人。譬之父兄師長。欲敎人以不淫。乃臚列其人其事。以爲某也如是之淫。淫者之語。如是其有情。則已不復成莊語矣。雖僮僕。亦應笑之。曾謂聖人而如是乎。且卽以淫詩。則不特伯叔君子與狂童狂且。一例無別。而旣見君子等語。反不若吉士誘之且舒而兌兌云云。亦何異於後世詞曲所謂悄悄冥冥潛潛等等者而必以爲被文王之化而必奪彼與此耶。則其說先已不可通矣。鄙意朱子注書甚多。或不無門人手作。則有小序無小序。或不足爲朱子輕重可耳。蘭公曰。朱子詩注。多云未詳。又卽本詩。略添一二虛字。便算是注。如必以朱子自注者。恐欲宗朱而反有累于朱也。又曰。南有喬木之注云。非復前日之可求矣。試問前日之求有何別耶。又曰。朱子無不是者。詩注恐出門人之作。力闇曰。弟年十二三時。讀至葛覃詩注。葛葉方盛而有黃鳥鳴于其上也。不覺大笑。此詩三句。一段萋萋叶喈喈則黃鳥自鳴于灌木之上耳。于葛葉何預。此雖其細已甚。然亦見其非出於朱子之手矣。此語從來無人說及。只鄙人以爲不然耳。又八月剝棗。十月穫稻二句。朱子音棗爲走叶。稻爲徒口反。而不知棗稻一韻。酒壽一韻。卽欲叶韻。則酒壽獨不可讀若湫濤乎。經中音切多誤。不可枚擧。此决爲朱子門人手筆。或晩年未定之本。非如學庸語孟之爲鐵板注疏也。必以其爲朱子而如手足之護頭目。遂無一語之敢議。亦過矣。自明迄今。大儒代有。皆以爲漢人去古未遠。皆尊小序。不容朱子一人起而廢之。凡屬鄭衛之詩。槩指爲淫奔之詩。而不知鄭衛之淫者。其音也而非詩也。此類辨甚多。一時不能記憶。惟高明詳察。余曰。此不可以口舌爭。請歸而詳覽諸敎。或有妄見。當以奉復也。此時酒行已餘十鍾矣。平仲發詩令分韻。余曰。弟不能詩。且不飮酒者。不必入於詩令。平仲見起潛飮酒曰豪哉。起潛曰。於此不用吾飮。惡乎用吾飮。待酒不來。先請詩。平仲曰。好好。如詩不成。罰依金谷酒數。起潛曰。我願罰。力闇曰。罰只三杯。不許多飮。起潛笑曰。一犯再犯三犯。皆笑。蘭公曰。詩成酒盡。悵如之何。諸人皆以小鍾。獨於平仲。以大椀勸之。平仲不辭。一飮而盡。起潛曰太速。余曰。東方飮法。自來如此。不如中國之約謹。時以大椀滿酙而進之。起潛亦一飮而盡曰何如。余曰。將與之角勝耶。起潛曰。爲歡耳。今日之飮。吾生平亦不多得也。平仲打圈于起潛之語。拊起潛之背曰。吾在東方。寧其獨醉。鮮與人飮酒樂矣。今日與兄輩相樂。非但吾輩之有光。抑兄輩之勝事。諸人皆笑。平仲曰。顧侯在坐。令人不樂。力闇曰。何謂所指耶。平仲曰。顧雍性嚴不飮酒。力闇笑曰。湛軒可謂時中之聖矣。時諸人皆醉矣。不必與之辨。故余亦笑曰。聖則吾不能。起潛指時中云云曰。太過。又曰。賢者在聖人之世。其仲弓夫子之流歟。余亦笑而不語。平仲謂起潛曰。俄謂吾兄與弟襟期相吻。今乃大覺兄不如我也。我則不動聲色而大器自來。兄則多般威喝而大器始來。兄我之以德以政。於此判矣。起潛笑曰。此東國中國之別也。平仲曰。如此則東國之幸。起潛曰。偶然耳。平仲曰。君子以德化人。吾兄以威制之。起潛笑曰。齊之以刑。不如道之以德。平仲熟視韓生曰。觀此兄亦好襟期也。韓生笑曰。襟期何好。但豪飮耳。力闇曰。若襟期不好。則京師之人如牛毛。弟亦不相與之矣。而彼亦安能望見顔色奔走若謁耶。一座皆笑。平仲謂力闇曰。見君之杯。可謂翺翔于蓬蒿之間矣。何必用管仲之器。或曰儉。孔子曰不知禮。力闇笑曰。我于管仲有何愛。愛見齊桓一口呑。盖取桓公之名小白也。起潛曰。我善養吾浩然之氣。其爲器也塞于天地之間。力闇曰。我只求早發。不願晩成。盖取大器晩成之語耳。平仲曰。我則能大能小。所謂君子不器也。起潛曰。狂語不須刪。此樂可忘死。小大亦不拘。能器吾許汝。平仲曰。所以吾不器。君則爭大小。起潛曰。大小且莫爭。只要不亂好。聖人學一半。止無量罷了。力闇曰。樂極。平仲曰。此樂莫爲醒者傳。起潛曰。聖人惟酒無量不及亂。卽此便是聖人。此事幷不由勉强故云天縱。平仲曰。雖無聖人語。我本不及亂。又曰。正聲何茫茫。力闇曰。邪話方袞袞。蘭公繼曰。酒氣實在香。力老殊荒唐。時又以燒酒繼之。平仲曰。味雖至好而雜飮之。則及其歸宿。迷於稅駕矣。幸二兄恕之也。諸人不聽。强勸不已。力闇蘭公。十餘鍾後不復飮。韓生已不勝而逃席。惟起潛與平仲痛飮不已。起潛益豪放。平仲已亂矣。諸人解衣盤礴。旁若無人。一言之發。滿座皆笑。起潛曰。今日不意竟有如此快聚。昨日之書。便如夢中語矣。始信天下事不可以意逆也。任天而動。必有得意處。何如。余笑曰。萬事分皆定。浮生空自忙。此時平仲頗不省事。余咎其不自量。且言于諸人。請愛人以德。遂輟去杯酌。平仲曰。樂已極矣。更以請誨嘉言。以畢其樂如何。蘭公曰。曲終奏雅。平仲曰。余亦談者。安知其必保其終也。起潛曰。所謂口頭禪。平仲曰。余非口頭禪。終不免於斯世之鄕愿耳。力闇曰。鄕愿卽村夫別名。平仲曰。鄕愿德之賊。而今日不可無王覇幷用矣。又曰。陸兄之字。醉不能記。亦可自反也。更示也。起潛笑曰。勿爲醒者傳。起潛曰。子靜於尊德性居多。某却於道問學居多。朱意如是矣。又曰。陸之學。亦有是否。余曰。朱子之所畏也。起潛曰。朱，陸分尊德性道問學。原本朱子。後人務尊朱而攻陸偏否。當日朱陸必無如此門戶見解。余曰。愚未見陸集。未知其學之淺深。不敢妄論。惟朱子之學則窃以爲中正無偏。眞是孔孟正脉。子靜如眞有差異。則後學之公論。無恠其擯斥。但名爲宗朱者。多偏於問學。終歸於訓詁末學。反不如宗陸之用功於內。猶有所得也。此最可畏耳。起潛曰。我不知學。於二家之學。亦幷未深究。但看後世宗朱宗陸。紛紛議論。全是血氣。而陸之後爲陽明。其事功炫赫。絶非空虛之事而人必詆之爲禪。其不爲禪者。乃絶無所表見。以外之事功而驗中之所得。良知亦未可盡非也。得兄之言。至爲持平心服矣。余曰。歸而思之。當有以反復也。平仲曰。弟則不知朱學陸學爲何如。而惟以入孝出恭愛君如父。爲一大公案。大抵聖道之爲宗。雖得其中。而末流之失傳。得其皮膚。各自爲岐。皆不能超然遠觀矣。弟在東夷。頗學古聖書。自不無慷慨之意耳。力闇始見平仲爲朱陸云云語曰。金兄亦思講學耶。恐不足當洪兄訶斥。盖日前。余以平仲之誤解謹獨。謂之大錯。力闇盖以此戲之也。蘭公曰。金兄不講學而所言已得聖賢下手處。虛談性命。誠何益也。平仲曰。兄安能識余不講學也。弟則已自許到聖域。舜何人我何人。一座大笑。力闇指到聖域云云曰。美哉美哉。平仲又曰。人之善惡。惟在一心而已。天性人皆所賦也而一欲字爲善惡。吾則得其善而已。一座又笑。力闇指惟在一心云云曰。此陸學也。又大笑。平仲又曰。前言皆戱耳。大抵人無私欲則百善皆明。人有私欲而專以文字相掩護。則相對未及深識。而分手之後。自有百世公論。兄必後思我而無及矣。雖無及矣。當奈何。一座又大笑。力闇又曰。我亦云然。又大笑。蘭公謂平仲曰。金兄何不日日過我一飮。起潛亦曰。明日過我飮乎。平仲曰。雖欲一日百過。何敢辭。或不無煩瑣之患耶。起潛曰。又作客氣語。公殆不可與飮者。平仲曰。弟何客氣終有所未妥。若無累於吾友。則弟何辭也。蘭公曰。先生若肯頻來飮。俗子相猜不足憂。是時。平仲脫帽解帶。攘臂揮筆。語無頭緖。余累次催歸而反以戱言加之。略不關聽。余以歸事關心。默坐不能言笑。力闇曰。純粹以精。洪兄是也。蘭公曰。時中之聖。余皆笑而不答。起潛知余催歸。謂余曰。老弟太不達情。何如是急。時。德裕已雇車待于門外。日已晩矣。余曰。去來皆有關由處。且金兄醉矣。尤難久坐。遂收篠飮詩稿綃畫及談草。蘭公向余有言。余未解聽。蘭公書卓上曰。盛德君子。余曰。兄之愚弄人如是。蘭公掉頭曰。不是不是。又書曰。賢者。余色頗不平。又書曰。然則金是狂兄是狷。一座大笑。余扶平仲登車。戒以歸臥。勿與人接。余入季父炕。適兩使會坐。余具告之故。且出詩畫。皆嗟異之。平仲少頃出來。語無倫次。副使覺之。謂余曰。君非愛人以德。余謝曰。誠如尊敎。但今日之事。不可以常理論之。副使還笑。無語。

When he had finished reading, Li'an's face overflowed with delight. He wrote in clerical script on the cover of the sheet: "Parting words of Master Damheon on leaving, shown to his descendants, to be treasured forever." Langong was stunned for a moment and then said, "This great instruction is truly medicine for the ailment. I shall revere it and wear it all my life." I said, "Because I love you two brothers keenly, my hopes for you are deep. The meaning lies in offering counsel; I did not dare give idle words of praise. Though my words are rough and clumsy, their meaning has support. I hope you will not reject the words because of the man."

Li'an said, "I shall respectfully take it as my lifelong 'leather and bowstring' to wear. But the words given to Brother Lan are deeply apt and plain; they are not only medicine for Brother Lan's ailment, and I too read them with a shudder. I further hope you will write a small sheet; it need not be fine paper, for I value only my brother's own hand. I would paste it at the right of my seat, so that it strikes the eye and alerts the heart, 'keep it in mind, it is here', and perhaps I may make a little progress; then the favour I receive from you will be greater still. Indeed I too am quite lacking in the two words 'dignity and gravity'." I said, "The ancients said that one must have it in oneself and only then demand it of others. If so, what one cannot do oneself can never be demanded of a friend? I ask you brothers to instruct me plainly." Langong said, "Admonition shows the ancients' sense of duty. But if you always follow it with modest words, that is still tinged with worldly sentiment." I said, "This is general talk of principle." Li'an said, "Even if it were truly as you say, one should not reject words because of the man; how much more with a brother whose sincerity within shows without." I said, "'Having it in oneself, then seeking it of others' I fear can run together with the principle of urging one another to good, without conflict. If, because one cannot do something oneself, one can never urge it upon a friend, would that not come close to harming one another? I think that in urging others, one is also spurred on oneself; this does not contradict the ancient meaning. What do you think?"

Li'an said, "Nowadays those who can encourage each other with the ancient principle are few; and even among those who lack it in themselves, few can say such words. You think you are demanding of others what you lack in yourself; I think you do have it in yourself and are seeking it of others. After this there is no need for much modesty." Qiqian said, "All is summed up in the two words 'urging to good'; there is originally no need to discuss having or lacking."

Pyeongjung had a poem that said: "Gold and jade is the man, with a heart of brocade and embroidery; / West Lake's elegant spirit is seen in Master Pan. / At the first examination you were raised early to fame; / When first welcomed at the guest lodge, the seat where we sat was fragrant. / I rejoice that this rare meeting must have been helped by fate; / I only pity that the fine gathering cannot last long. / All my life when parting I have never shed tears; / Today with you I shed them in the evening sun." Pyeongjung said, "This is a poem for parting from Brother Pan; I hope you will give me your criticism." Langong said, "Both the poem and the feeling bring tears to the eyes. But the first four lines cannot escape being overpraise." Qiqian laughed and said, "Now, when you see a girl, do you too put on a girl's airs?" (This was because Langong's looks resembled a woman's.) Everyone laughed greatly.

Li'an said, "These two sheets are for other people who admire your calligraphy. However many characters, write as you please in one sweep to answer them, and sign your honoured name." Pyeongjung said, "What are you saying? My brushwork is ugly and crude; it can only express feeling." Before he had finished, the two pressed him earnestly without stop, and I too urged him. Pyeongjung then wrote, in half-lines, a Tang quatrain on each sheet, and everyone praised them without end. Pyeongjung said, "I could not disobey your order. Setting myself up as a good calligrapher and sweeping the brush at will, is there another such wild and rash person in the world? You two brothers have made your foolish brother show his horse's hoof completely and have not spared him at all. I am rather vexed." Langong laughed loudly and said, "We wanted you to do just that, to provide some laughter and jest." Li'an said, "I think Zhang Zhangshi [Zhang Xu] could not have surpassed it." Langong jested again, "You say 'horse's hoof'; with your wonderful wrist, are you competing with a thoroughbred's feet?" Pyeongjung said, "I rashly uttered the two words 'horse's hoof', and I accept them willingly." Langong said, "Your writing has the force of chasing the wind and pursuing lightning; 'horse's hoof' is an exquisite comment, not a rash word."

Pyeongjung said to Li'an, "The 'Record of Nurturing the Void' you favoured me with the other day can be called words that, thrown to the ground, ring like metal and stone. But in the Eastern country the national ban is extremely strict, and the single character 'wine' does not circulate within the country at all. Having received my brother's writing, I wish not only to hide it deep in my book-box as a treasure to pass down but also to show it off to others and talk of it with those who understand; this is the common human feeling. I do not know what to do." Li'an said, "Then shall I compose another piece, avoiding the word 'wine'? Why must wine be avoided? The Analects mentions wine more than once; was Confucius wrong, then?" Pyeongjung said, "The 'wine' of 'fond of wine' need not be changed; but the 'wine' of 'drinking wine' absolutely must not be cut down and left vague, not stated plainly." Li'an said, "In prose, ebb and flow allows some borrowing; but if the lofty fun of the drinking side is removed, the interest is much reduced. This morning Brother Lu also singled out this passage for praise; to remove it would seem to lessen the flavour." Qiqian said, "Without mentioning the national ban, how about saying only that recently he has given up drinking?" Pyeongjung said, "The two words 'given up drinking' are not honest." Qiqian said, "Then nothing can be done."

Li'an said, "Brother Kim loves wine, yet the national ban is so strict. How do you get through the days?" Pyeongjung said, "Living is worse than dying." Qiqian laughed loudly and said, "A wine-ghost!" The whole room laughed. Li'an said, "How sad, how sad. It would be fortunate to die quickly and be reborn in China." Langong said, "If you are reborn in China, you should be born in Zhejiang, where there is Shaoxing wine and you could drink every day." Qiqian said, "I too wish to travel east like that. I take Haedong to be a White Lotus Society." Li'an said, "Brother Kim must often drink in secret. I shall report him, and that is why I exposed his vice in the Record." Everyone laughed. Langong said, "In my letter the other day I said 'use only the vessel of Guan Zhong'; today may I ask to use Guan Zhong?" Pyeongjung said, "Not only the vessel of Guan Zhong; even the use of a shell-ladle and bamboo tube, nothing can be done." And he said, "Bound by the national ban, I dampen my own enjoyment; it is sad."

Qiqian said, "Does Brother Hong not let a drop touch his lips?" I said, "I have never drunk; it is not merely observing the ban." Qiqian said, "Then do you also dislike others drinking?" I said with a smile, "I myself do not drink; how could I dislike others drinking? I only dislike those who disregard the national ban." Everyone laughed. Qiqian said, "The one who wrote the Lisao was by nature alone sober." Langong said, "How about drinking secretly today?" Pyeongjung said, "Brother Hong always warns me against it, so with Brother Hong present I dare not speak of wine. But today even Brother Hong can do nothing about me." Qiqian said, "At banquets, how do you make merry?" I said, "For more than ten years the country has suffered repeated bad harvests, and the ban on wine has been very strict. But it is after all not something to be banned forever, so many who love it drink in secret, since the offence does not amount to a capital crime. At banquets no one dares to use it openly. Because of this the times are desolate and there is little of the pleasure of worldly flavour. But nothing can be done." Qiqian said, "Have there recently been abundant years as well?" I said, "In recent years there have not been great failures, but since the ban has been in force so long, it is for the time being not changed from the old."

I said, "Today's meeting cannot be merry without wine. Though there is a national ban, we are already outside the borders, and there may be a way of acting by expedience. As for Brother Kim, though I need not urge him to drink, I would not wish to pull him back and stop him either. A wine-ghost easily haunts a man like a nightmare; if we let him get drunk just once and have done with it, so much the better. (The wording of the last clause is obscure in the source.)" Everyone laughed. Qiqian said, "In that case you permit it. After drinking, would it do to see the three Excellencies?" I said, "When there is an extraordinary gathering under heaven, one should respond with an extraordinary deed under heaven; how can one hold to a single theory?" Langong said, "The Elder of Joy [wine] has arrived. Please put down the brush and ink." Then vegetables, fruit and several dishes of meat soup were set on the table, and a small cup was placed before each of us. The servants warmed the wine and poured it.

At that moment a guest arrived. I rose and wished to step down, but all pulled me back and stopped me. The guest at once took a seat. Langong said, "This is Brother Han from Shanxi; hearing your names, he has come to visit." Li'an said, "This Shanxi friend is also a fellow lodger here for the metropolitan examination." I exchanged greetings with him briefly in speech. The man was startled and said to Li'an, "He can speak our language too!" [spoken in colloquial Chinese] Li'an made some reply, in general saying that the characters are the same but the sounds differ, and that the difference of local speech is the same for them and for us. Qiqian said, "How much can Brother Kim drink before he is drunk?" I said, "His capacity is quite wide, but a few cups and he is drunk, and he utters many wild words." Pyeongjung said, "His wildness cannot be matched." Qiqian said, "Cigong was wild when sober [an allusion to Gai Kuanrao of the Han, courtesy name Cigong]; why must it be wine?" Pyeongjung said, "I am wild when I do not drink; after drinking, on the contrary, I am not wild."

Qiqian said, "What kind of wine did Haedong have in former days? Is it something like the distilled liquor of the 'red-haired' people?" I said, "The Eastern country has much rice, so its wine too is praised as fine. There are various kinds, such as 'red dew', each with its own name. The one called 'Gyedang wine' (the second character of the name is rare, perhaps for 'sugar', i.e. a cinnamon-sugar liquor; uncertain) is very strong, and those fond of drinking it are often harmed." Pyeongjung said, "In general the wine of the Eastern country is fierce and strong, twice as much as China's." Qiqian said, "Recently genuine Jiaozhi cinnamon has become extremely expensive. Are the 'ox-hide paste' and 'clear-heart pills' made in Haedong made with genuine Jiaozhi cinnamon?" I said, "True cinnamon bark has long been entirely cut off. We merely substitute thick-skinned bark; all of it is bought in the capital market. How can one tell genuine from false?" Qiqian said, "Thick-skinned bark is not valued here; we all prize thick flesh." I said, "Is there still genuine cinnamon in the south?" Qiqian said, "The genuine is truly hard to get. The thick-skinned cinnamon we absolutely dare not use here in treating illness, so its use is very small. The genuine leads fire back to its source; the false stirs up fire. What is used in the Eastern country is not genuine cinnamon, so does using it not stir up fire?" I said, "Even if there is no visible harm, who knows whether it does not grow in secret and unseen?" Qiqian said, "The Eastern country's medicinal materials are all bought from China, and there are also separate local products." I said, "Those from local products may be six or seven in ten." Qiqian said, "How many days do you voyage by sea? Is it not hard?" Pyeongjung said, "In the former dynasty the Liaodong road was blocked, so we went by sea. Now we only cross the Yalu River. From the capital it is about three thousand seven hundred li." Qiqian said, "How far is it to Liaodong?" I said, "More than five hundred li." Qiqian said, "In the Eastern country's book collections, are the Veritable Records of the former dynasty and the unofficial histories quite complete?" I said, "Books such as the Ming History and the 'Benmo' have mostly gone out to us; there may be some unofficial histories as well."

At this time each drank and poured as he pleased from small cups. Langong himself took a cup, placed it before me and urged me, "Please drink three cups; I dare not urge more." I said, "I have never drunk. There is no need to force me. Besides, I only know the taste in wine; why must it be the thing in the cup?" Qiqian said, "I will drink in your place." Everyone laughed. Pyeongjung said, "To drink in place of Brother Hong means you want to drink double. Brother Hong and I came together; you want to seize Brother Lu's 'government' of today [the sense is uncertain; perhaps mastery of the drinking]." Qiqian said, "Then shall I drink for Brother Kim as well?" The whole room fell about laughing. I called for tea. Each time the others drank wine, I always called for tea in its place, saying, "With tea in place of wine, my elegance is swept away completely."

Qiqian said, "Your robe is open on all four sides; is it also a former Ming style?" I said, "This is military dress. It seems to be a Ming style, but I dare not say so definitely. Officials' court dress and scholars' Daoist robes are in general inherited from Ming styles." Li'an said, "Your letter of the other day I have not answered for a long time; in the end I shall surely reply. The Minor Prefaces must on no account be abolished. In his annotations to the Odes Zhu Xi has in fact many blunders and inconsistencies; I dare not agree." Langong said, "Zhu Xi's abolition of the Minor Prefaces mostly derives from Zheng Yuzhong." I said, "Who is Yuzhong?" Langong said, "His name is Qiao, his style Jiaji, a man of Fujian; he wrote the Tongzhi." I said, "As for the Minor Prefaces, I do not dare to follow earlier statements, nor to cover for Zhu Xi; but when I look at his words they are indeed without evidence. I hope you will explain in detail to dispel my ignorance."

Qiqian said, "That you, younger brother, follow Zhu Xi is quite right. But in abolishing the Minor Prefaces, he surely could not avoid forced interpretation." Langong said, "Take for instance the poem 'The White Colt': Zhu Xi's note says 'the fine guest is still wandering free'. Zhu Xi's notes of this kind are extremely numerous. Is that indeed right?" I said, "In exegesis there is probably room for regret, but in the end it does not hide the goodness of his larger body of work." Qiqian said, "That example is small, but there are very many of this kind. Taking the Minor Prefaces as the topic: Ma Duanlin attacked Zhu with all his strength, and his argument was most incisive. In my humble view, the Minor Prefaces were not far from antiquity and seem to have a source. The ancients passed on teaching from master to disciple in a single line of transmission, like the three schools of Gao [sic; evidently a copying error for Qi], Lu and Han, each with its source; in fact they parted ways and went in different directions, yet at the time they were preserved and none was abolished in the academies. This shows not only the ancients' reverence for the classics but also the principle of transmitting what is credible as credible and what is doubtful as doubtful. Zhu Xi decided on his own view and for the first time abolished the Minor Prefaces. In fact elsewhere he follows the Minor Prefaces quite often; only for the poems of Zheng and Wei, relying on the one phrase 'the sounds of Zheng are licentious', did he consign them all together as licentious poems. 'The sound is licentious, not the poem'; the ancients already argued this. If they are taken as licentious, then Confucius's editing of the Odes was originally to teach people. It is like fathers, elder brothers and teachers who wish to teach people not to be licentious, and so list that person and that deed, saying that so-and-so was this licentious, and that the speech of the licentious was so full of feeling; then it is no longer solemn speech, and even servants would laugh at it. Can one say a sage would do so? Moreover, taking them as licentious poems, not only are 'uncles and gentlemen' and 'wild boy, wild fellow' treated alike with no distinction, but when 'gentleman' and similar words have been seen, it is the reverse of 'the fine man lures her, and she is slow and yielding' and so on. How is that different from what in later ci and qu are called 'qiaoqiao, mingming, qianqian' and so on, and yet one insists that they were touched by King Wen's civilising influence and necessarily 'takes from that to give to this' (that is, shifts poems arbitrarily from one category to another)? Then that theory is already unworkable at the outset. In my humble view, Zhu Xi annotated very many books, and some may well be the work of disciples; so whether there is or is not a Minor Preface may not carry weight for Zhu Xi, that is all."

Langong said, "In Zhu Xi's annotations to the Odes he often writes 'not yet understood'; and sometimes he simply adds one or two particles to the poem's own text and counts that as the annotation. If one insists they are Zhu Xi's own annotations, I fear that wishing to honour Zhu one would instead burden him." He also said, "The note on 'In the south there are tall trees' says 'it can no longer be sought as before'. May I ask: what difference was there in the seeking of former days?" He also said, "Zhu Xi has nothing that is wrong; so the annotations to the Odes probably came from the work of disciples." Li'an said, "When I was twelve or thirteen and read the note on the poem 'Ge Tan', where it says 'the dolichos leaves are just luxuriant and there is a yellow bird singing above them', I laughed out loud involuntarily. In that poem the three lines form one section: 'luxuriant' rhymes with 'twittering', so the yellow bird is simply singing on the bushes; what has it to do with the dolichos leaves? Though this is extremely small, it also shows that the note did not come from Zhu Xi's hand. Nobody has ever said this; only I think otherwise. Again, in the two lines 'In the eighth month they strike the jujubes; in the tenth month they reap the rice', Zhu Xi gives the sound of 'jujube' as 'zou' by rhyme-adjustment and of 'rice' as 'tu-kou fan'; but he does not know that jujube and rice are one rhyme, and 'wine' and 'longevity' another. If he wanted to adjust rhymes, then why could 'wine' and 'longevity' alone not be read like 'qiu' and 'tao'? The sound glosses in the classics are full of errors, too many to list. This is surely the work of Zhu Xi's disciples, or a late, unfinished text; it is not like the commentaries to the Great Learning, the Mean, the Analects and Mencius, which are 'iron plates'. To protect him as one protects one's head and eyes with hands and feet, simply because he is Zhu Xi, so that no one dares to voice a single criticism, is also going too far. From the Ming until now great Confucians have appeared in every generation, and all consider that the men of Han were not far from antiquity and all honour the Minor Prefaces, and do not allow Zhu Xi alone to rise and abolish them. All poems belonging to Zheng and Wei he generally designates as poems of licentious elopement, not knowing that what is licentious in Zheng and Wei is their music, not their poems. There are many arguments of this kind; I cannot remember them all at once. I only ask your lofty discernment to examine them in detail."

I said, "This cannot be argued with the tongue. Let me go back and read your instruction in detail; if I have some presumptuous views I shall reply." By now the wine had gone round more than ten cups. Pyeongjung proposed a poetry game with assigned rhymes. I said, "I cannot write poetry, and I do not drink; there is no need to include me in the poetry game." Pyeongjung, seeing Qiqian drink, said, "How heroic!" Qiqian said, "If not here, where else shall I use my drinking? While the wine has not yet come, ask first for the poem." Pyeongjung said, "Good, good. If the poem is not finished, the penalty will follow the Golden Valley wine-count." Qiqian said, "I am willing to be penalised." Li'an said, "The penalty is only three cups; you are not permitted to drink more." Qiqian smiled and said, "First offence, second offence, third offence." All laughed. Langong said, "When the poem is done and the wine is finished, how disappointing that will be." The others all drank from small cups, but to Pyeongjung alone they offered a large bowl. Pyeongjung did not refuse and drained it in one gulp. Qiqian said, "Too fast." I said, "The Eastern way of drinking has always been so, not as restrained and careful as in China." Then a big bowl was filled and offered to Qiqian; he too drained it in one go and said, "How was that?" I said, "Are you going to compete with him for victory?" Qiqian said, "Only for joy. Today's drinking is one I have not had many of in my whole life."

Pyeongjung drew circles on Qiqian's words [in approval] and patted Qiqian on the back, saying, "In the East I would rather get drunk alone, and I rarely drink in joy with others. Today's joy with you brothers is not only an honour for us but also a fine event for you." Everyone laughed. Pyeongjung said, "With Lord Gu present, it makes one unhappy." [Gu Yong of the Three Kingdoms was a teetotaller; the jibe is aimed at Hong.] Li'an said, "Whom do you mean?" Pyeongjung said, "Gu Yong was strict by nature and did not drink wine." Li'an laughed and said, "Damheon can be called a sage of timeliness." By now everyone was drunk and there was no need to argue with them, so I too smiled and said, "A sage I cannot be." Qiqian pointed at the phrase about timeliness and said, "That is too much." He also said, "A worthy man living in a sage's age: Zhonggong, the sort of disciple of the Master, perhaps?" I smiled too and said nothing.

Pyeongjung said to Qiqian, "A while ago I said that you and I were matched in spirit, but now I am keenly aware that you are not my equal. I, without moving a muscle, have the large vessel come of itself; you, with all manner of shouting and threats, only then get the large vessel to come. Between ruling by virtue and ruling by government, you and I are judged here." Qiqian laughed and said, "This is the difference between the Eastern country and China." Pyeongjung said, "If so, it is the Eastern country's good fortune." Qiqian said, "It is chance." Pyeongjung said, "A gentleman transforms people by virtue; you restrain them by awe." Qiqian laughed and said, "To regulate them by punishments is not as good as to lead them by virtue." Pyeongjung stared hard at Mr Han and said, "Looking at this brother, he too has a fine spirit." Mr Han laughed and said, "What fine spirit? Merely heavy drinking." Li'an said, "If his spirit were not good, people in the capital are as many as ox hairs; I would not associate with him either, and how could he hope to see my face and rush to pay a call?" The whole room laughed.

Pyeongjung said to Li'an, "Seeing your cup, one can say it is soaring among the weeds. Why use the vessel of Guan Zhong? Someone said, 'Was he frugal?' Confucius said he did not know the rites." Li'an laughed and said, "What do I love in Guan Zhong? I love to see Duke Huan of Qi swallowed in one mouthful," taking Duke Huan's name, Xiaobai ["Little White"]. Qiqian said, "I am good at nurturing my flood-like qi; as a vessel it fills the space between heaven and earth." Li'an said, "I only seek to bloom early; I do not wish for late attainment," taking the saying "a great vessel is completed late". Pyeongjung said, "I can be big or small; this is what is called 'the gentleman is not a vessel'." Qiqian said, "Wild talk need not be deleted. This joy can make one forget death. Big or small, no constraint. If you can be a vessel, I allow you." Pyeongjung said, "That is why I am not a vessel; you are the one who quarrels over big and small." Qiqian said, "Let us not quarrel over big and small; we need only not be disorderly. The sage learned by halves: he stopped at 'no limit', and that was all." Li'an said, "Joy at its extreme." Pyeongjung said, "This joy must not be passed on to the sober." Qiqian said, "The sage had no limit only in wine, but did not reach disorder. Just this is a sage. This matter does not come from effort, hence it is said to be heaven-endowed." Pyeongjung said, "Though I have no sage's words, by nature I do not reach disorder." He also said, "The correct sound, how vast and dim!" Li'an said, "Wicked talk now rolls on and on." Langong followed, "The smell of wine is truly fragrant; Old Li is utterly absurd."

Then distilled liquor followed. Pyeongjung said, "Though the taste is excellent, if I mix my drinks, when it comes time to go home to rest I shall be lost as to unyoking the carriage. I hope you two brothers will excuse me." The others did not listen and urged him without stop. Li'an and Langong did not drink again after about ten cups. Mr Han, unable to hold it, fled the table. Only Qiqian and Pyeongjung drank heartily without stopping. Qiqian grew more and more bold and unrestrained; Pyeongjung was already disorderly. They took off their robes and sat sprawling, as though no one else were there; whenever one said a word the whole room laughed. Qiqian said, "I never expected today to have such a delightful gathering. Yesterday's letter now seems like words in a dream. I finally believe that the affairs of the world cannot be anticipated by the mind. Moving as heaven wills, one is bound to find something satisfying. What do you say?" I smiled and said, "All things are fixed by lot; floating life busies itself in vain." At this time Pyeongjung was quite out of his senses. I blamed him for overestimating himself and told the others, asking them to love a man by virtue; so the cups were put away.

Pyeongjung said, "Joy has reached its extreme. Let us instead ask for good words of instruction to complete the joy." Langong said, "When the tune ends, play the elegant." Pyeongjung said, "I am also one who talks; who knows that I shall keep it to the end?" Qiqian said, "What is called mouth Zen." Pyeongjung said, "I am not mouth Zen; in the end I cannot escape being a 'village worthy' of this age." Li'an said, "'Village worthy' is another name for a country bumpkin." Pyeongjung said, "The village worthy is the thief of virtue, but today we cannot do without using the kingly and hegemonic ways together." He also said, "Brother Lu's courtesy name: I am drunk and cannot remember it, which I can reflect on in myself. Show it again." Qiqian laughed and said, "Do not pass it on to the sober." Qiqian said, "'Zijing's teaching lies mostly in honouring the moral nature; mine, on the contrary, lies mostly in the path of inquiry and study.' Such was Zhu Xi's meaning." He also said, "Does Lu's learning also have right and wrong?" I said, "It is what Zhu Xi feared."

Qiqian said, "The division of Zhu and Lu into honouring the moral nature and the path of inquiry and study originally comes from Zhu Xi. Later people strive to honour Zhu and attack Lu, biased and wrong. In their own day Zhu and Lu surely did not have such sectarian views." I said, "I have not seen the collected works of Lu and do not know how deep or shallow his learning is; I dare not discuss it rashly. But as for Zhu Xi's learning, I privately consider it central, upright and unbiased, truly the correct line of Confucius and Mencius. If Zijing really differed, the public judgement of later scholars in rejecting him is not strange. But those named followers of Zhu are mostly biased toward study and end up in philology, a minor learning; this is, on the contrary, worse than the followers of Lu, who apply effort inward and still gain something. This is the most to be feared." Qiqian said, "I do not know learning, and I have not studied either school deeply. But looking at the later followers of Zhu and of Lu, their confused arguments are all temper. After Lu came Yangming, whose achievements shone; they were certainly not empty matters, yet people insist on slandering him as Chan. Those who are not Chan have nothing to show at all. If one tests inner attainment by outward achievement, 'innate knowing' cannot be wholly rejected either. Your words are most fair, and I am convinced." I said, "I shall go home and think it over; I shall surely reply again."

Pyeongjung said, "I do not know what Zhu-learning or Lu-learning may be; I take only 'at home be filial, abroad be respectful, love the ruler as a father' as one great case. In general, the Way of the sages is the principle; though one may get its centre, the later streams lose the transmission, get only its skin, and each go off into branches, all unable to look from a transcendent distance. I, in the Eastern barbarian land, have studied the ancient sages' books a fair amount and cannot be without some feeling of ardour." Li'an had first seen Pyeongjung's remarks about Zhu and Lu and said, "Brother Kim also thinks of lecturing on learning? I fear he may not withstand Brother Hong's rebuke." (For the other day I had said that Pyeongjung's misreading of 'being watchful when alone' was a great error, and Li'an was teasing him with this.) Langong said, "Brother Kim does not lecture on learning, yet what he says has already reached where the sages and worthies begin; empty talk of nature and destiny, what real use is it?" Pyeongjung said, "How can you know that I do not lecture on learning? I have already granted myself arrival at the sage's realm: 'Who was Shun, and who am I?'" The whole room laughed greatly. Li'an pointed at 'arrival at the sage's realm' and said, "Beautiful, beautiful." Pyeongjung said further, "People's good and evil lie only in the one heart. Heavenly nature is endowed in everyone, and the single word 'desire' makes good or evil; I take only the good." The room laughed again. Li'an pointed at 'lie only in the one heart' and said, "This is Lu-learning." There was great laughter again.

Pyeongjung said further, "My earlier words were all jest. In general, if people have no selfish desire, then the hundred goods are all clear. If people have selfish desire and use only words to cover for one another, then face to face one has not got to know them deeply, and after parting, there will be the public judgement of a hundred generations. You will surely think of me later, and it will be too late. Even if too late, what will you do?" The whole room laughed greatly again. Li'an said, "I say the same", and there was great laughter again. Langong said to Pyeongjung, "Why does Brother Kim not visit me for a drink every day?" Qiqian also said, "Will you visit me for a drink tomorrow?" Pyeongjung said, "Even if it were a hundred visits a day, how dare I decline? But perhaps there would be the trouble of burdening you." Qiqian said, "Again polite talk. You are probably not one fit to drink with." Pyeongjung said, "How is it polite? There is still something that is not quite proper; if it brings no burden to my friends, why would I decline?" Langong said, "If you are willing to come often to drink, there is no need to worry about vulgar people's suspicion."

At this time Pyeongjung took off his hat and loosened his belt, rolled up his sleeves and wielded the brush, his words without thread. I urged leaving several times, but he only answered me with jests and did not listen at all. With my mind on returning, I sat silently and could not talk or laugh. Li'an said, "'Pure and refined': Brother Hong is that." Langong said, "A sage of timeliness." I laughed and did not answer. Qiqian, knowing that I was urging departure, said to me, "Younger brother, you are too unaccommodating of feelings; why such hurry?" By then Deokyu had hired a cart and was waiting outside the gate, and the day was already late. I said, "There are reasons for coming and going; moreover Brother Kim is drunk, and it is all the harder to sit long." So I gathered Xiaoyin's poem drafts, the silk paintings and the conversation drafts. Langong said something to me which I could not follow. Langong wrote on the table, "A gentleman of abundant virtue." I said, "Brother, you make fun of people like this!" Langong shook his head: "No, no." He wrote again, "A worthy." My face turned rather displeased. He wrote again, "Then Kim is the 'wild' and you are the 'fastidious'." The whole room laughed. I helped Pyeongjung into the cart, warned him to go home and lie down and not to meet people. I entered my uncle's kang, where the two envoys happened to be sitting together. I told them the whole reason and showed them the poems and paintings; they all sighed in wonder. Soon Pyeongjung came out, his speech incoherent. The Vice-Envoy noticed and said to me, "You are not loving him through virtue." I apologised: "Truly as you say. But today's matter cannot be judged by ordinary principles." The Vice-Envoy smiled in return and said nothing.
